blocks.content: Imagine you’re building a ticket booking system.
Two users try to book the last available seat at the same time. Your system needs to check availability, reserve the seat, and confirm the booking.
Now think about this: what if both users see the seat as available and both end up booking it? Or one user reads old data while another is updating it?
This is where transaction isolation levels come into play. They control how multiple transactions interact with each other and what kind of data each transaction is allowed to see.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785282762414-209561174.png
blocks.alt: Sequence diagram of two users racing to check availability and reserve the same seat, showing why transaction isolation levels matter

blocks.content: Isolation levels define how much visibility and interference is allowed between transactions from very loose (faster but risky) to very strict (safe but slower).
1. How data is stored  pages and heap files
blocks.text: 1. How data is stored  pages and heap files

blocks.content: A database doesn't write one row at a time to disk. It organises data into fixed-size pages (typically 8 KB in PostgreSQL). A page is the smallest unit the database reads and writes. All rows live inside pages, and pages live inside heap files.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399130293-648032883.png
blocks.alt: How data is stored pages and heap files

blocks.content: When you query a row, the DB loads its entire page into the buffer pool(memory cache).

["If the page is already in memory fast. 
","If not disk read slow. 
"]
items: If the page is already in memory fast.

blocks.content: This is why the buffer pool size matters: a larger pool means more pages cached, fewer disk reads.
2. Indexes (the most important performance tool )
Without an index, every query scans every page in the heap file from start to finish a sequential scan. With an index, the DB jumps directly to the relevant pages. The difference is O(n) vs O(log n).
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 441 — without an index on user_id, the DB reads every single row in the orders table (could be millions) just to find the 12 rows belonging to user 441.

blocks.content: B-Tree index how almost every index works
blocks.text: B-Tree index how almost every index works

blocks.content: A B-Tree (Balanced Tree) is a self-balancing tree where every leaf node is at the same depth. The tree stores key values in sorted order with pointers to the actual heap pages containing the rows.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785282765001-72884062.png
blocks.alt: Diagram of a B-Tree index walking from the root node through an intermediate node down to a leaf node that points to the actual data page

blocks.content: When you search for user_id = 441, the database doesn’t scan everything. Instead, it starts at the root node, which contains ranges like [250 | 500]. Since 441 lies between 250 and 500, it moves to the middle child node.
In the next level, it checks [300 | 400 | 450]. Now it compares again 441 is between 400 and 450, so it follows the correct path further down.
Finally, it reaches the leaf node, which directly points to where the actual data is stored (Page 7, slot 3). The database then loads that page and retrieves the row.
This process takes only a few comparisons (logarithmic time), which is why indexes are extremely fast compared to scanning the entire table.

-- Without index: full table scan
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 441;
-- Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0..18450 rows=1 width=80)
-- Filter: (user_id = 441)
-- Rows read: 500,000

-- Add index
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user ON orders(user_id);

-- Now: index scan
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 441;
-- Index Scan using idx_orders_user
-- Index Cond: (user_id = 441)
-- Rows read: 12   ← night and day

3. Query execution ( parse, plan, execute )
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024005-995998303.png
blocks.alt: Diagram of the four internal query execution stages a SQL query goes through: parse, rewrite, plan, and execute

blocks.content: When you fire a SQL query, it goes through four internal stages before a single row is returned.
1. Parse
SQL string is tokenised and converted into an abstract syntax tree (AST). Syntax errors caught here.
2. Rewrite
Views are expanded, rules applied. A SELECT * FROM user_orders becomes the actual underlying query if user_orders is a view.
3. Plan (query planner / optimiser)

The most important stage. The planner generates multiple execution plans and picks the cheapest one using table statistics row counts, column cardinality, index availability. This is why ANALYZE keeps statistics fresh.
4. Execute
The chosen plan runs. Rows flow through operators: SeqScan → Filter → Sort → Limit. Each operator is a pipeline stage.

-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the actual plan chosen
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT
  u.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE u.city = 'Mumbai'
GROUP BY u.name;

-- Output (simplified):
-- HashAggregate (cost=1240..1280)
--   → Hash Join (cost=840..1200)
--       → Seq Scan on users
--           Filter: city = 'Mumbai'
--       → Index Scan on orders (idx_orders_user)
-- Planning time: 0.8ms
-- Execution time: 12ms

blocks.content: 4. Write-Ahead Log (WAL)

Every write in a database touches two places: the WAL (an append-only sequential log on disk) and the buffer pool (in-memory pages). The WAL is written first always. This is what makes writes crash-safe.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399130293-85988400.png
How a database ensures durability using WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) during a transaction.
blocks.text: How a database ensures durability using WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) during a transaction.

blocks.content: When a transaction runs and reaches commit, the database does not directly write changes to the main data pages on disk.
Instead, it first writes all the changes to a special log file called the WAL. This write happens sequentially and is followed by an fsync() call to make sure the data is physically stored on disk.
Once the WAL is safely written, the database confirms the commit to the client. At this point, the transaction is considered durable even if the actual data pages are still in memory.

If the system crashes after the WAL is written, the database can recover by replaying the WAL during restart, restoring all committed changes. If the crash happens before the WAL is written, the transaction is simply discarded (rolled back), as it was never officially committed.
Meanwhile, the actual data pages are updated later in the background (via buffer pool and checkpoints). This makes the system efficient while still guaranteeing that no committed data is ever lost.
The WAL also powers replication. PostgreSQL streaming replication ships WAL records to replica servers in real time.
The replica replays the same log it becomes an exact copy of the primary. This is how read replicas work.
5. Concurrency ( locking vs MVCC )
Multiple queries run simultaneously. The database must prevent them from corrupting each other's work. There are two broad approaches.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399130609-492884771.png
Two ways databases handle concurrency: Pessimistic Locking and MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control).

["In Pessimistic Locking, the database locks a row before reading or updating it. When a transaction runs a query like SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, it acquires a lock on that row. 
"]
items: In Pessimistic Locking, the database locks a row before reading or updating it. When a transaction runs a query like SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, it acquires a lock on that row.

blocks.content: While this lock is held, no other transaction can modify that same row they must wait. This guarantees no conflicts, but it can slow things down because transactions block each other, especially under high load.

["In MVCC, the database takes a different approach. Instead of locking, it creates multiple versions of the data. 
"]
items: In MVCC, the database takes a different approach. Instead of locking, it creates multiple versions of the data.

blocks.content: Each transaction sees a snapshot of the database as it existed when the transaction started. So even if another transaction updates the data and commits, the first transaction still sees the old value.
This means readers don’t block writers and writers don’t block readers, making the system much more scalable. Old versions are cleaned up later by background processes.
In short, pessimistic locking prioritizes safety by blocking, while MVCC prioritizes performance by allowing parallel access using data versions.

MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)is how PostgreSQL lets reads and writes run simultaneously without blocking each other. Every row has a hidden x min and x max column storing which transaction created and deleted it.
A query only sees rows where x min≤ its snapshot and x max is either null or greater than its snapshot.
6. Row-store vs column-store
The two fundamentally different ways data can be laid out on disk and the choice determines what kind of queries are fast.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399130610-486657748.png
1. Row Store (OLTP)
In row-based storage, data is stored row by row. That means all fields of a record (id, name, city, age) are kept together.
When you query something like:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 2;

the database can quickly fetch the entire row in one go because everything is stored together. This makes row stores very efficient for transactions like inserts, updates, and fetching individual records.
However, if you run an analytical query like:
SELECT avg(age) FROM users;
the database still has to read all rows and all columns, even though you only need the age column. This makes it slower for large-scale analytics.
Best for: OLTP (transactions, real-time apps)
2. Column Store (OLAP)
In column-based storage, data is stored column by column. All values of a single column (like ages) are stored together.
So for a query like:
SELECT avg(age) FROM users;
the database reads only the age column and ignores everything else. This makes it extremely fast for aggregations and analytics.
It also compresses data very well because similar values are stored together.
But if you want a full row (like all details of a user), the database has to fetch data from multiple columns and combine them, which is slower.
Best for: OLAP (analytics, reporting, dashboards)
